vignette: A 19-year-old woman felt her heart start pounding suddenly while bending to tie her shoelaces. She is otherwise well.
hints: Narrow or broad? Regular or irregular?
Regular, narrow, very fast, no visible P waves, sudden onset.
explanation: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at about 185/min with no visible P waves (they are buried in or just after the QRS). Sudden onset and offset in a young, well person fits AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia, the commonest regular SVT, and one that is more common in women.
features: Rate about 185/min, perfectly regular
Narrow QRS
No P waves visible before the QRS
pearl: In AVNRT, look for a 'pseudo-r′' in V1 or 'pseudo-S' in the inferior leads: the retrograde P wave hiding at the end of the QRS.

vignette: An 82-year-old woman feels exhausted and dizzy. Pulse 38 and regular.
hints: Mark the P waves and march them out. Then do the same for the QRSs.
P waves and QRS complexes each keep their own regular rate and ignore each other.
explanation: P waves march through regularly at about 88/min, broad QRS complexes march at about 38/min, and the PR interval is random because nothing conducts. That is complete (third-degree) heart block with a ventricular escape rhythm. A narrow escape would suggest a higher, junctional escape, which is faster and more reliable.
features: P waves regular at about 88/min
Broad escape QRS regular at about 38/min
No consistent PR: complete AV dissociation
P waves hide in QRS and T waves
pearl: In complete heart block the atria beat faster than the ventricles. If the ventricles are faster, think of another cause of AV dissociation, such as VT.

vignette: A 63-year-old man with a heart attack two years ago has palpitations and feels light-headed. BP 92/60.
hints: Is the QRS narrow or broad?
Regular, broad, fast, and a scarred heart. Put it together.
explanation: A regular broad-complex tachycardia at about 175/min with identical QRS complexes. With a past MI, a broad-complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise. Clues to AV dissociation clinch it: P waves marching through at their own slower rate, and capture or fusion beats.
features: Rate about 175/min, regular
Broad QRS (about 165 ms), all the same shape
Dissociated P waves visible here and there
pearl: Assume any broad-complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise. After a previous MI, the vast majority are.

vignette: World Stroke Day. A 74-year-old woman with high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes says her smartwatch keeps flagging an irregular pulse.
hints: Try to find one clear, repeatable P wave. Go on.
Measure a few R-R intervals. Is there any pattern at all?
explanation: An irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm with no identifiable P waves and a wavy fibrillatory baseline: atrial fibrillation. Fitting for World Stroke Day: AF raises stroke risk around five-fold, and about one in four strokes is linked to it. Age, high blood pressure and diabetes all add to that risk, which is why scores like CHA₂DS₂-VA exist.
features: Irregularly irregular R-R intervals
No P waves; fine fibrillatory baseline
Narrow QRS, rate about 100/min
pearl: Irregularly irregular with no P waves is AF until proven otherwise. MAT is also irregular, but it has P waves in at least three different shapes.

vignette: A 34-year-old woman ran the New York City Marathon yesterday and is having a routine check with her sports doctor. She feels well; her resting pulse is slow and a little irregular. Lead II rhythm strip:
hints: Look at the PR interval, beat by beat.
The PR stretches, then one P wave stands alone with no QRS.
explanation: The PR interval lengthens with each beat (about 190, 290, then 340 ms) until a P wave fails to conduct; the cycle then resets with the shortest PR. That gives grouped beating. The block is usually in the AV node, so it is often benign in athletes, during sleep and with high vagal tone, though drugs and inferior MI can cause it too.
features: Progressive PR prolongation
Then a non-conducted P wave (dropped QRS)
Shortest PR straight after the pause; grouped beating
pearl: Compare the PR just before and just after the dropped beat. Different: Wenckebach. Identical: think Mobitz II.

vignette: A 63-year-old woman has had 40 minutes of heavy central chest pain spreading to her jaw. She is sweaty and nauseated. 12-lead ECG:
hints: Which leads are elevated, and which leads mirror them?
ST elevation in III bigger than II, with ST depression in aVL.
explanation: ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal ST depression and T inversion in aVL (and I): an inferior STEMI. Elevation in III greater than II points to the right coronary artery. Reciprocal change argues strongly against pericarditis. Right-sided leads (V4R) look for right ventricular involvement.
features: ST elevation in II, III and aVF (III > II)
Reciprocal ST depression and T inversion in aVL and I
Early Q wave forming in III
pearl: Reciprocal depression in aVL is often the first clue to an inferior STEMI, sometimes before the inferior elevation is obvious.

vignette: A 46-year-old woman notices her heart 'skipping' when she drinks coffee at work. Lead II rhythm strip:
hints: Some beats are wide, early and have no P wave.
Count how often they come: two normal beats, then one odd one.
explanation: Every third beat is an early, wide, bizarre QRS with no preceding P wave and a compensatory pause: a premature ventricular complex (PVC) in a 2:1 pattern, called ventricular trigeminy.
features: Two sinus beats, then a PVC, repeating
PVCs are wide with no P wave
Full compensatory pause after each PVC
pearl: Occasional PVCs in a healthy heart are common and usually benign. Very frequent PVCs (over about 10% of beats), symptoms or structural heart disease deserve an echo and a Holter.

vignette: A 66-year-old woman on haemodialysis has missed two sessions and now feels weak, with palpitations.
hints: Look at the shape of the T waves: tall, narrow and pointed.
Then look at the P waves and the QRS: flat and wide.
explanation: Tall, narrow, symmetrical 'tented' T waves, flattened P waves, a long PR (about 230 ms) and a widening QRS. The classic sequence as potassium rises: peaked T waves, then PR prolongation and P-wave flattening, then QRS widening, then a sine-wave pattern, VF or asystole. The ECG is a poor guide to the actual level and can deteriorate quickly.
features: Tall, narrow, peaked T waves (V2–V4, II)
Flattened, broad P waves; PR about 230 ms
QRS widening (about 135 ms)
pearl: Hyperacute T waves of a STEMI are broad-based and bulky. Hyperkalaemic T waves are narrow-based and pointed, like a tent.

vignette: A 34-year-old woman, two weeks after a long-haul flight, has sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. HR 112, SpO2 91%.
hints: Look at lead I and lead III together.
Sinus tachycardia plus T inversion in V1 to V3 points to right ventricular strain.
explanation: Sinus tachycardia with a deep S wave in lead I, a Q wave and inverted T wave in lead III (S1Q3T3), and T-wave inversion in V1–V3: a pattern of acute right ventricular strain, consistent with pulmonary embolism in this story.
features: Sinus tachycardia
S1Q3T3
T-wave inversion V1–V3
pearl: The commonest ECG finding in PE is just sinus tachycardia; S1Q3T3 is specific but insensitive. A normal ECG doesn't rule PE out. Use Wells/PERC and imaging.

vignette: A 34-year-old woman on methadone, recently started on a macrolide antibiotic, suddenly collapses. The ward monitor shows:
hints: Look at the beats before it started. Check the QT.
Polymorphic VT whose QRS amplitude twists around the baseline.
explanation: Sinus beats with a very long QT, then an early beat lands on the T wave and triggers a fast polymorphic broad-complex tachycardia whose amplitude waxes and wanes, appearing to twist around the baseline. That is torsades de pointes, a polymorphic VT driven by QT prolongation, here from two QT-prolonging drugs. Low potassium and magnesium add fuel.
features: Long QT in the preceding sinus beats
Polymorphic VT at about 230/min
Amplitude waxes and wanes: 'twisting of the points'
pearl: A QTc over 500 ms markedly raises torsades risk, especially when QT-prolonging drugs (methadone, macrolides, ondansetron, some antipsychotics) are combined.

vignette: A 68-year-old man with high blood pressure has an ECG as part of a health check. He feels well.
hints: Work out the axis first: look at leads I and II.
Lead II is mostly negative, but the QRS is narrow.
explanation: Narrow QRS with marked left axis deviation (lead I positive, lead II negative): small r and deep S in II, III and aVF (rS) and qR in I and aVL. That's left anterior fascicular block (left anterior hemiblock).
features: Left axis deviation (about −50°)
rS in II, III, aVF
qR in I and aVL, narrow QRS
pearl: LAFB is the commonest cause of left axis deviation. With RBBB it makes bifascicular block, and adding a long PR is sometimes called 'trifascicular block'.

vignette: A 67-year-old woman with diabetes has ongoing chest pain. Troponin is rising.
answer: Aslanger pattern (inferior MI with multivessel disease)
options: Aslanger pattern (inferior MI with multivessel disease)
ST elevation in aVR with widespread ST depression
hints: ST elevation in only one inferior lead.
Add the ST elevation in V1 and the lateral ST depression with upright T waves.
explanation: ST elevation in lead III only (not II), ST depression in V4–V6 with positive T waves, and ST elevation in V1 greater than in V2: the Aslanger pattern, an inferior occlusion MI masked by coexisting multivessel disease.
features: ST elevation in III but not II
ST depression V4–V6 with upright T
ST elevation in V1 greater than V2
pearl: Not every occlusion MI meets STEMI criteria. Patterns like Aslanger, de Winter and posterior MI need urgent cath-lab discussion. Treat the patient, not just the millimetres.

vignette: A 63-year-old woman with diabetes has had heavy chest discomfort and nausea for an hour.
hints: Which leads have ST elevation, and which have the mirror image?
I, aVL, V5 and V6 look at the same wall.
explanation: ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6 with reciprocal ST depression in III and aVF: lateral STEMI, often from the circumflex or a diagonal artery.
features: ST elevation I, aVL, V5–V6
Reciprocal ST depression III and aVF
Ongoing ischaemic symptoms
pearl: Women and people with diabetes more often present with atypical symptoms such as nausea, breathlessness or fatigue rather than classic pain. Lateral STEMIs are easy to miss because the ST elevation in aVL can be small.
